title: Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) Part Five: Conformance Criteria and Examples
summary: The fifth and final MIME document. It describes MIME conformance criteria and gives examples of MIME messages, along with acknowledgements and the bibliography.

eli5.summary: This is the checklist that says what an email program must do to count as MIME-ready, plus worked examples.

questions: what must a mime compliant mail client do
what is the mime canonical encoding model
why do email gateways corrupt messages
subtitle: The checklist that says what a mail program must do to count as MIME-ready, plus the model behind MIME encoding.

tldr.problem: MIME lets mail carry non-ASCII text, attachments and multi-part bodies, but the mechanisms are open-ended, and no program is expected to support every media type. Mail also passes through old gateways and mail servers that mangle data.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2049 lists ten things a MIME-conformant mail user agent must do, warns about eight ways mail gets damaged in transit, and describes a four-step canonical model for encoding a body.
tldr.outcome: A conformant program can safely receive almost any properly labelled data, because anything it does not understand is treated as undifferentiated binary and not splashed onto the screen. The RFC obsoletes RFC 1521, RFC 1522 and RFC 1590.

facts.label: Safe line length
facts.value: Lines over 76 characters may be wrapped or truncated

sections.title: Where This Document Fits
sections.content:
RFC 2049 is the fifth and final document in the MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) set. MIME redefines message bodies so that mail can carry text in character sets other than US-ASCII, non-text formats, multi-part bodies and non-ASCII text in headers. The four earlier parts are RFC 2045 (header fields), RFC 2046 (media types), RFC 2047 (non-ASCII text in headers) and RFC 2048 (registration procedures).

This part does three jobs. It defines what a MIME-conformant implementation must support, it describes pitfalls of contemporary messaging systems, and it presents the canonical encoding model that MIME is based on. It also gives an example message, a summary of changes from the earlier documents, and the bibliography. It obsoletes RFC 1521, RFC 1522 and RFC 1590.
sections.eli5: MIME is the set of rules that lets email carry pictures and other languages. This last part is the rulebook's checklist and a few examples.

sections.title: What a MIME-Conformant Mail Program Must Do
sections.content:
The RFC says it is not expected that every implementation supports every media type. Instead it defines a minimum level, called MIME-conformance, that allows useful interworking with content that differs from US-ASCII text. A mail user agent that is MIME-conformant MUST meet ten requirements.

  • Always generate a MIME-Version: 1.0 header field in any message it creates.
  • Recognize Content-Transfer-Encoding and decode quoted-printable and base64, and also recognize the identity encodings 7bit, 8bit and binary. Non-7bit data sent without encoding must be labelled 8bit or binary. Because SMTP does not support those, a sender over SMTP must encode and label the data, for example as quoted-printable or base64.
  • Recognize and interpret Content-Type, avoid showing users raw data of a type other than text, ignore content type parameters it does not recognize, and be able to send at least text/plain with the charset parameter when it is not US-ASCII.
  • Treat an unrecognized transfer encoding, or an unrecognized content type, as application/octet-stream.

The remaining requirements cover specific media types, the handling of non-MIME mail, and encoded-words in headers.

Text
Display US-ASCII text, tell the user what any other character set is, and show at least the characters with octet values 1-127 for ISO-8859-* sets. Unknown character sets are treated as application/octet-stream.
Image, audio, video
Treat unrecognized subtypes as application/octet-stream.
Multipart
Recognize mixed, alternative (avoid showing redundant parts) and digest (default part type message/rfc822). Treat unrecognized subtypes as mixed.
Message
Recognize and display message/rfc822 so that recursive structure is preserved. Treat unrecognized subtypes as application/octet-stream.

Conforming agents may offer non-standard support for non-MIME messages in non-US-ASCII character sets on received messages only. They must not send non-MIME messages containing anything other than US-ASCII text, and MUST label anything other than plain US-ASCII text with proper MIME headers. They must also recognize encoded-words in headers, supporting both the B and Q encodings for any character set they support.

The payoff, in the RFC's words, is that it is assumed to be safe to send virtually any kind of properly marked data to users of such systems, because they will at least treat it as undifferentiated binary and will not simply splash it onto the screen.
sections.eli5: A mail program that is MIME-ready always says what is in each message, and when it meets something it does not understand, it saves it as a plain file instead of showing garbage.

sections.title: Guidelines for Sending Email Data
sections.content:
Internet email is not a perfect, homogeneous system. Mail may travel across many networking technologies, and some do not support the full functionality of the SMTP environment. The RFC notes many widely deployed non-conformant mail transfer agents that alter messages on the fly. It gives eight guidelines for designing a data format that must survive the widest range of networks and broken servers. The persistence of each of the following must not be relied on:

  • CRLF as anything other than a line break, since encodings may be converted between base64 and quoted-printable.
  • Isolated CR and LF characters, because systems use plain CR, plain LF, CRLF or counted records for newlines.
  • NUL characters (value 0), which are problematic largely because C library routines use NUL as a terminator.
  • TAB characters, which may become variable numbers of spaces. This is strongly discouraged but may occur.
  • Lines longer than 76 characters, which may be wrapped or truncated. Applications that need long lines must distinguish soft from hard line breaks, for example by using quoted-printable.
  • Trailing white space, which may be removed or padded.

Two more guidelines concern characters. Across character-converting gateways such as EBCDIC systems (the RFC mentions BITNET), the only characters known to be consistent are the 73 made up of the letters A-Z and a-z, the digits 0-9, and eleven special characters. A maximally portable representation sticks to short lines and these 73 characters, and the base64 encoding follows this rule. Finally, some servers corrupt certain literal strings: a period alone on a line, and a line starting with From (with a trailing space). A careful composer can encode these, for example as =2E and =46rom in quoted-printable.

These are not recommended practices for mail servers. RFC 821 servers are prohibited from altering white space or wrapping long lines. The practices are known to occur on real networks, and implementations should be robust against them.
sections.eli5: Mail is passed along by many helpers, and some of them smudge the message, like a game of telephone. So the rules say what you should not count on staying exactly the same.

sections.title: The Canonical Encoding Model
sections.content:
Earlier versions were confused about when data is converted to canonical form and encoded, especially for CRLFs, because newline representation varies by system. This document therefore models composing a MIME entity as four steps, done for each innermost-level body:

  1. Creation of local form. The body is created in the system's native format, character set and line-ending convention.
  2. Conversion to canonical form. The body, including out-of-band information like record lengths, is converted to a universal canonical form that depends on the media type. For text/plain the text must be in a supported character set with CRLF line delimiters.
  3. Apply transfer encoding. An appropriate Content-Transfer-Encoding is applied. There is no fixed relationship between media type and transfer encoding, so the choice may depend on character frequency counts in a given body.
  4. Insertion into entity. The encoded body goes into a MIME entity with headers, which is then inserted into a higher-level entity (message or multipart) as needed.

Reversing the steps converts an entity back to local form, but the original and final local forms are not guaranteed to be the same.

The RFC stresses this is only a model, not a blueprint. Real systems may fold canonical conversion into the encoder, or pass encoder output through further steps. But the resulting messages must be consistent with those the model would produce. For example, a body labelled Content-type: text/foo; charset=bar with Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64 must first be represented as text/foo, then in the bar character set, and finally base64 encoded.

Formats that use local newline conventions are not canonical MIME. They are instead encodings of RFC 822 in which CRLF is encoded as the local newline. A format that encodes CRLF as LF cannot represent MIME messages with binary data containing LF octets that are not part of CRLF line separation.
sections.eli5: Think of packing a gift: make it, put it in a standard-size box, wrap it for the post, then put the parcel in a bigger parcel. The person opening it undoes the steps in reverse.

sections.title: A Complex Multipart Example
sections.content:
Appendix A outlines a message of five parts displayed one after another: two introductory plain text parts, an embedded multipart message, a text/enriched object, and a closing encapsulated text message in a non-ASCII character set. The embedded part is multipart/parallel, so its two objects, an audio fragment and a JPEG picture, are displayed at the same time.

The example shows several features. The top-level type is multipart/mixed with a boundary parameter. A part with a blank line straight after the boundary has no header fields, which means US-ASCII text, while the next part says the same thing with explicit typing. The final part is message/rfc822 whose own body is ISO-8859-1 text in quoted-printable. Text before the first boundary, the preamble, is meant for readers that do not understand multipart and is ignored by those that do.
sections.eli5: It is a parcel with boxes inside boxes. Some things in it are shown one by one, and a picture and a sound are shown together.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 1521, 1522 and 1590
sections.content:
Appendix B lists 32 changes from the earlier MIME documents. The set was completely reformatted and split into multiple documents to improve the plain text version, which is required to be the reference copy. BNF for the overall header structure was added, while the type-specific BNF for the seven media types was removed as incorrect, incomplete and inconsistent.

Notable technical changes include these:

  • The definitions of 7bit and 8bit were tightened so that bare CR and LF can only be used as end-of-line sequences, and NUL characters are no longer required to be preserved.
  • Canonical text now requires CRLF line breaks, with CR and LF not allowed elsewhere.
  • multipart/digest support was added to the minimum conformance list, and the message/rfc822 requirement was strengthened.
  • The image/gif definition was moved to a separate document because of potential conflicts with IETF rules on patented technology.
  • Examples using text/richtext were changed to text/enriched.
sections.eli5: This is the list of what was fixed since the last rulebook, such as being stricter about line endings.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document adds no security section of its own. It says only that security issues are discussed in the second document of the set, RFC 2046. Appendix B notes that security issues specific to message/external-body are now discussed in some detail there.

One conformance rule has a protective side effect: a conformant agent avoids showing users raw data of types it does not understand, and treats unknown content as opaque binary, so that data never intended as text is not displayed as text.
sections.eli5: The safety rules are in another part. The checklist here helps by making programs save mystery files instead of showing them.

viz.caption: THE FOUR STEPS OF THE CANONICAL ENCODING MODEL

items.title: 1. Local form
items.text: The body is created in the system's native format and newline convention.

items.title: 2. Canonical form
items.text: Converted to the universal form for its media type, such as CRLF line breaks for text/plain.

items.title: 3. Transfer encoding
items.text: A Content-Transfer-Encoding such as base64 or quoted-printable is applied.

items.title: 4. Entity insertion
items.text: The encoded body gets headers and is placed in a message or multipart entity.
